action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum anti-GluN1 positive (1:80); sodium 134 and potassium 3.4 mmol/L; CK 198 U/L; low-titer ANA with negative anti-dsDNA; THC on the urine screen; beta-hCG negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain the serum work-up (blood count, chemistry, thyroid function and antibodies, HIV, beta-hCG, serum anti-GluN1 cell-based assay read with the CSF)
action_criteria.rationale: Screens metabolic, toxic, infectious, thyroid and lupus-related causes of the change from her usual bipolar episodes and gives the serum anti-GluN1 result, which supports but cannot replace the CSF assay.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Subtle bilateral caudate head FLAIR signal; medial temporal lobes normal; no enhancement
action_criteria.label: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination; a normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes before LP in a patient with new vacant stares and chorea; it is normal or non-specific in most patients and does not confirm the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Near-normal CSF (5 cells/mcL, no oligoclonal bands), HSV PCR negative, CSF anti-GluN1 IgG positive (1:32)
action_criteria.label: Analyze CSF for cells, protein and glucose, OCB/IgG index, HSV PCR and a cell-based IgG anti-GluN1 assay interpreted in parallel with serum
action_criteria.rationale: The CSF cell-based anti-GluN1 assay establishes definite disease even when the routine CSF is near normal, and the HSV PCR addresses the infectious mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Generalized slowing with bilateral temporal polymorphic delta; no seizures recorded on the artifact-limited routine study
action_criteria.label: Obtain EEG for encephalopathic and epileptiform abnormalities, explicitly assessing for extreme delta brush
action_criteria.rationale: Vacant stares, echolalia and orofacial movements need an electrographic assessment; an abnormal EEG separates encephalitis from a mood episode.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left ovarian 4.1 cm mature cystic teratoma
action_criteria.label: Perform pelvic and abdominal ultrasound to screen for an ovarian teratoma
action_criteria.rationale: Women of reproductive age carry the highest teratoma risk; tumor removal is part of first-line treatment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Seizure burden and evolution of the background over 24 hours or more
action_criteria.label: Escalate to continuous EEG monitoring to quantify seizure burden and detect non-convulsive seizures
action_criteria.rationale: The routine study was limited by artifact and she has vacant stares, so monitoring is needed to detect non-convulsive seizures.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Avoid valproate or halve lamotrigine; keep lamotrigine without gaps; quetiapine with risperidone adds QTc and extrapyramidal risk
action_criteria.label: Check her lamotrigine, quetiapine and risperidone against the acute agents
action_criteria.rationale: She takes lamotrigine and two antipsychotics, and the antiseizure choice and the antipsychotic plan both depend on the interactions.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General published evidence on anti-NMDAR encephalitis diagnosis and immunotherapy
action_criteria.label: Optionally review published evidence on anti-NMDAR encephalitis diagnosis and immunotherapy
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only: no diagnostic or management step of this case depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1 to 2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the left ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynecology.

Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant and with lamotrigine on board (or halve the lamotrigine dose); continue lamotrigine without interruption; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for autonomic instability (labile blood pressure with diaphoresis, heart rate 118 bpm) and electrographic seizures, with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first; stop risperidone and taper quetiapine, and monitor CK and temperature.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management; gynecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: CSF HSV PCR negative; medial temporal lobes normal on MRI; no fever beyond 37.8 °C; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel and onconeural antibodies negative; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Bipolar disorder relapse (mood episode with psychotic features)
differential.key_features: Her psychiatrist judges the episode atypical: echolalia, stereotyped face rubbing, orofacial movements, chorea, vacant stares, autonomic lability, seizures and extreme delta brush on continuous EEG, and CSF anti-GluN1 antibodies, none of which a mood episode explains; therapeutic lamotrigine level.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-related encephalopathy (cannabis-induced psychosis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome)
differential.key_features: Occasional cannabis does not explain chorea, seizures or CSF antibodies; for NMS, tone is normal without rigidity, CK is only 198 U/L and temperature 37.8 °C, and the illness began before quetiapine was increased and risperidone added.
ANA 1:80 only, with negative anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm, normal complement and no systemic features; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

key_clinical_evidence: Ten to eleven days of insomnia, grandiosity and paranoia that became atypical for her bipolar episodes, with echolalia, stereotyped face rubbing, orofacial movements and chorea, vacant stares, and labile blood pressure with diaphoresis, five weeks after a sore throat and fatigue: at least four of the six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:32) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016), even with a near-normal routine CSF; serum positive 1:80 is read with the CSF.
MRI shows only subtle caudate head FLAIR signal with normal medial temporal lobes; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
The routine EEG shows slowing, and continuous EEG captures two right temporal seizures and extreme delta brush; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a 4.1 cm left ovarian mature cystic teratoma: its removal is part of first-line treatment.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumor removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013); her lamotrigine and two antipsychotics shape the antiseizure and agitation plan.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A psychiatric history does not protect against autoimmune encephalitis; echolalia, stereotypies, orofacial movements, chorea and autonomic instability are atypical for a mood episode and call for the encephalitis work-up.
red_herrings.data_point: Known bipolar disorder type II, with the episode first attributed to hypomania by her psychiatrist.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a bipolar relapse and delays the neurologic work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing (SIADH from another cause, dehydration, polydipsia) instead of recognizing SIADH as a known complication of NMDAR-E.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Occasional cannabis use three days earlier explains the screen but not chorea, orofacial movements, seizures, autonomic instability or CSF antibodies.
red_herrings.data_point: Urine drug screen positive for THC metabolites.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: NMS needs rigidity and a markedly raised CK; tone is normal and the CK barely raised. The illness preceded the antipsychotic changes; stop risperidone and watch CK and temperature.
red_herrings.data_point: Recent quetiapine increase and risperidone, with CK 198 U/L, tachycardia and temperature 37.8 °C.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Invites a diagnosis of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A low-titer ANA is common in healthy young women; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are negative, complement is normal and there are no systemic features.
red_herrings.data_point: ANA 1:80 (speckled) with a maternal aunt with SLE.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure 14 cmH2O. WBC 5 cells/mcL (100% lymphocytes), protein 36 mg/dL and glucose 60 mg/dL (CSF/serum ratio 0.64). No oligoclonal bands; IgG index 0.55 (normal). Gram stain: no organisms; culture: no growth at 48 hours. HSV and VZV PCR not detected. Anti-NMDA receptor (GluN1) IgG positive on cell-based assay, titer 1:32. Clinical correlation recommended.

special_tests.NMDAR_antibodies: Positive, titer 1:32 (cell-based assay, IgG anti-GluN1; reference laboratory, resulted day 6)

alternatives: Lorazepam for agitation and insomnia in place of further antipsychotic doses.
contraindications: Class warning: haloperidol and other high-potency dopamine D2 antagonists are associated with severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic malignant-like reactions in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
Valproate: avoid in women able to become pregnant unless other options fail.
interactions: Lamotrigine with valproate: valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles the lamotrigine level, raising the risk of serious rash (SJS/TEN) and toxicity; the lamotrigine dose must be halved if valproate is ever combined.

Lamotrigine: abrupt withdrawal can provoke seizures and mood relapse, and a gap of more than about five half-lives needs re-titration from the starting dose because of the rash risk; give doses by nasogastric tube if she cannot take them by mouth.
Lamotrigine with estrogen-containing contraceptives: the estrogen lowers the lamotrigine level; relevant if contraception is started before cyclophosphamide.
Quetiapine with risperidone: additive QTc prolongation, sedation, orthostatic hypotension and anticholinergic effects; risperidone also adds extrapyramidal and neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk.
Quetiapine and risperidone with lorazepam: additive sedation and respiratory depression.
High-dose methylprednisolone: hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and corticosteroid-induced mood elevation; monitor potassium and mental state.
IVIG: no pharmacokinetic interaction with lamotrigine, quetiapine or risperidone; risk of renal impairment and thrombosis, so ensure hydration.
IV acyclovir: no relevant interaction; maintain hydration given poor oral intake.
Levetiracetam: no pharmacokinetic interaction with lamotrigine or the antipsychotics.
general.summary: Lamotrigine, quetiapine and risperidone reviewed against the acute agents: valproate doubles lamotrigine, lamotrigine must not lapse, and the two antipsychotics add QTc, sedation and extrapyramidal risk. Class cautions listed above.
warnings: Rituximab: screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before the first dose.
Cyclophosphamide is gonadotoxic and teratogenic: discuss fertility preservation and contraception.
Hypokalemia (potassium 3.4 mmol/L) adds to the QTc risk of the two antipsychotics; correct it.

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosis and treatment

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titers related more closely to outcome than serum titers.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumor, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumor removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Extreme delta brush was found in 7 of 23 adults with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumor removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

patient.history_present_illness: A 25-year-old left-handed woman with a 2-year history of bipolar disorder type II, well-controlled on lamotrigine and quetiapine, was brought to the ED by her psychiatrist after failing to respond to adjustments in her psychiatric medications over the past 9 days. Her psychiatrist describes her as having been in remission for 14 months prior to this presentation. The behavioral change began approximately 10-11 days ago with worsening insomnia, grandiosity, and pressured speech, initially attributed by her psychiatrist to a hypomanic episode. Over the following days, however, the psychiatric symptoms became more severe and atypical for her prior episodes, including features of paranoia (believing she was being surveilled by her neighbors), visual illusions (seeing 'shadows moving'), and on two occasions echolalic speech that was noted by her mother. She also developed a new repetitive behavior of pulling at her hair and rubbing her face in a stereotyped fashion, which her psychiatrist recognized as abnormal for a bipolar episode. Her psychiatrist increased quetiapine to 200 mg and added risperidone 1 mg without improvement. She has had no witnessed generalized seizures. She did not have a recent febrile illness but did report a period of severe fatigue and mild sore throat about five weeks ago. Her weight has dropped 4 kg over the past 10 days due to refusal to eat. Lamotrigine level was checked two days ago and was within therapeutic range. The psychiatrist is concerned this is not a typical bipolar episode and has referred her to the ED for further evaluation.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild autonomic instability: diaphoresis, tachycardia, blood pressure lability between 118-142 systolic during 2-hour observation. Mild pyrexia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 4mm. Extraocular movements intact. No nystagmus. Facial sensation intact. Orofacial region: intermittent lip pursing and chewing movements noted.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed safely due to agitation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, markedly agitated and non-cooperative. Speech is echolalic at times. Orientation cannot be reliably assessed. Grandiose statements made ('I'm writing a book that will change the world'). Intermittent stereotyped facial rubbing noted. Brief vacant stares lasting 10-20 seconds observed twice during interview.
neurological_exam.motor: Full strength bilaterally. Mild bilateral upper extremity choreoathetotic movements, subtle but present. Tone normal; no rigidity.
